name: Frontend Developer Roadmap
tagline: From HTML and CSS to fast, accessible, real-time web applications
summary: An ordered path for building modern web frontends. It begins with the three languages of the browser and the protocols that connect it to a server, moves into a typed component framework with state, routing and testing, and ends with the delivery concerns — performance, accessibility, rendering strategy, CDNs, authentication and real-time updates — that separate a demo from a product.

steps.label: HTML, CSS & JavaScript
steps.note: Every framework compiles down to these three; semantic HTML, layout with CSS and the JavaScript event loop are non-negotiable basics.

steps.label: Git & version control
steps.note: Branching, pull requests and reviewing diffs are part of the daily workflow before your first team project.

steps.label: HTTP
steps.note: Fetching data, caching headers, CORS and status codes all come from HTTP; understanding it explains most network-tab mysteries.

steps.label: REST APIs
steps.note: Frontends spend most of their time consuming APIs, so learn how resources, methods and error responses are conventionally shaped.

steps.label: TypeScript
steps.note: Types catch a large class of bugs at compile time and make component props and API responses self-documenting as the codebase grows.

steps.label: React (or another component framework)
steps.note: Components, props and rendering-on-state-change are the mental model every modern framework shares; learn one deeply.

steps.label: State management
steps.note: As apps grow, deciding what is local, shared, or server state (and caching server responses) becomes the main source of complexity.

steps.label: Routing
steps.note: Client-side routing, nested layouts and URL-as-state turn a page into an application without full reloads.

steps.label: Testing
steps.note: Unit tests for logic, component tests for behaviour and a few end-to-end tests let you refactor the framework code you just wrote with confidence.

steps.label: Build tools & bundlers
steps.note: Knowing what Vite, esbuild or webpack do to your code (bundling, tree-shaking, code splitting) is the prerequisite for measuring performance.

steps.label: Web performance
steps.note: Core Web Vitals, lazy loading and bundle size directly affect users and search ranking; measure before you optimise.

steps.label: Accessibility (a11y)
steps.note: Keyboard navigation, ARIA and contrast are cheapest to get right while components are being built, not retrofitted later.

steps.label: Caching
steps.note: Browser cache, service workers and client-side data caches decide how fast a repeat visit feels and how stale it may be.

steps.label: CDN
steps.note: Static assets and even rendered pages are served from the edge; understanding CDN caching completes the picture you started with HTTP headers.

steps.label: SSR / SSG & rendering strategies
steps.note: Choosing between client rendering, server rendering and static generation is a trade-off of performance, freshness and infrastructure cost.

steps.label: Authentication in the browser
steps.note: Cookies vs tokens, secure storage, OAuth redirects and CSRF are frontend concerns as much as backend ones.

steps.label: WebSocket
steps.note: Chat, collaboration and live dashboards need the server to push; WebSocket gives a persistent two-way channel.

steps.label: Server-Sent Events
steps.note: For one-way streams (notifications, AI token streaming) SSE is simpler than WebSocket and works over plain HTTP — know when each fits.
